extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of literary criticism; translators and critics of poetry and classical texts
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance for literary criticism of poets (e.g., Heine) and for translating/classifying ancient moral texts (e.g., Marcus Aurelius) — focusing on voice, moral quality, tone, fidelity, and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic authorial voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Heine never attempts to be 'hubsch objectiv', 'beautifully objective'... he always remains Heinrich Heine, a son of the nineteenth century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force impersonation of historical personae or archaic mindsets; preserve the writer's own distinct voice and century-specific sensibility when evaluating or reproducing work. Example: Heine writes varied historical characters but never becomes an 'old Egyptian' or 'an old Hebrew' in spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Width of range / variety of figures
rubrics_metrics.description: One has only to turn over the pages of his Romancero ... to see Heine's width of range; the most varied figures succeed one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value a poet's ability to range over many subjects, characters, and historical figures while maintaining coherence. The presence of varied figures (kings, poets, adventurers) is a mark of range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of irony and modern tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe how the irony of the whole of that, finishing with the grim innuendo ... is at once truly masterly and truly modern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the effectiveness of ironic tone: modern, cutting irony that culminates in a pointed innuendo indicates mastery. Look for an ironic finish that reframes preceding description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of form (Greek) and intensity/sublimity (Hebrew)
rubrics_metrics.description: By his perfection of literary form, by his love of clearness, by his love of beauty, Heine is Greek; by his intensity, by his untamableness, by his 'longing which cannot be uttered,' he is Hebrew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize works that combine refined form/clarity with passionate intensity; the union of beauty of expression and sublime fervor is presented as a high poetic ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility in portrayal (comic and serious sides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heine shows us his own people by its comic side; in the poem of the Princess Sabbath he shows it to us by a more serious side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an author can depict subjects in multiple registers — comedic, satirical, solemn — without collapsing into caricature. Versatility of tone is a strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of plaintive / melancholy strains
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor must Heine's sweetest note be unheard—his plaintive note, his note of melancholy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and value melancholy or plaintive passages as part of a poet's emotional range; such strains can be central to the work's effect, especially in exile or dying-author contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral balance and nobleness of soul as critical criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: He is only a brilliant soldier in the Liberation War of humanity. ... A half-result, for want of moral balance, and of nobleness of soul and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the artist's moral character and 'self-respect' when judging adequacy as an interpreter of the modern world; persistent moral defects (intemperance, unscrupulous attacks, lack of generosity) are counted against ultimate greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral writings must supply inspiration/emotion (not only rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paramount virtue of religion is, that it has lighted up morality; that it has supplied the emotion and inspiration needful for carrying the sage along the narrow way perfectly, for carrying the ordinary man along it at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral or religious writing, judge whether it furnishes not only principles but also the joyful, motivating emotion necessary to move ordinary people to practice. Dry, purely intellectual precepts are inadequate for the masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat antiquity as living and modernly applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Long treats Marcus Aurelius's writings ... not as a dead and dry matter of learning, but as documents with a side of modern applicability and living interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful translator/commentator should render ancient texts as sources of present interest and practical instruction; emphasize contemporary relevance in notes and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity, substantiality, and precision in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantiality, soundness, and precision of Mr. Long's rendering are ... conspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations should be faithful and accurate to the original thought; sound scholarship and precision of sense are essential criteria for judging translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional courtesy in criticising predecessors
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of taste, a translator should deal leniently with his predecessor; ... Mr. Long's language is a great deal too hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or writing about translations, maintain generous/temperate language toward prior translators; harsh dismissals are discouraged as a matter of taste and collegiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture spirit and vigor (warmth of feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeremy Collier's warmth of feeling gave to his style an impetuosity and rhythm which from Mr. Long's style ... are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Besides literal accuracy, value a translation's ability to convey the original's spirit, rhythm, and emotional warmth. Sometimes an earlier, less literal version may better catch the author's force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of competence in the source language
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeremy Collier's real defect as a translator is not his coarseness and vulgarity, but his imperfect acquaintance with Greek; this is a serious defect, a fatal one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholarly competence in the original language is essential; inadequate knowledge of the source tongue is a fatal flaw in translation regardless of stylistic merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and idiomatic plain language for general readers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential to render him in language perfectly plain and unprofessional, and to call him by the name by which he is best and most distinctly known. The translators of the Bible talk of pence and not denarii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing the general public, translators/editors should use idiomatic, plain language and familiar terms/names rather than pedantic or scholastic forms; adapt currency, names, and technical terms for reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to prioritize content or form based on original
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only are the contents here incomparably more valuable than the external form, but this form, the Greek of a Roman, is not exactly one of those styles which have a physiognomy ... The Greek of Thucydides and Plato has this charm ... but the Greek of Marcus Aurelius ... is wanting in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the original's stylistic 'physiognomy' is essential; if not, a translation that emphasizes clear content over reproducing awkward form may be preferable. For authors whose style is a vital part of the effect, prioritize form when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extract clear thought from obscure wording and reproduce suitable tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Long has firmly seized upon the clear thought which is certainly at the bottom of that troubled wording, and, in distinctly rendering this thought, has at the same time thrown round its expression a characteristic shade of painfulness and difficulty which just suits it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A translator should interpret obscure or corrupt passages to reveal the underlying clear thought, and render it in English with an expression that preserves the original's appropriate tonal shade (e.g., painfulness, difficulty).
